newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU criteria must be met for stable euro - Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: EMU criteria must be met for stable euro - Tietmeyer.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer on Saturday reiterated his call for convincing and sustainable adherence to the criteria EU states must fulfil to take part in Europe's planned currency union.

In the text of a speech to a group of German property owners, Tietmeyer said the euro should enhance the European trade market, create more efficient capital markets and should mean a strong role for the currency on the world stage.

But he added: "The euro will only really bring these advantages if it remains lastingly stable and if currency union does not lead to economic tensions or even political conflict among participating countries."
Tietmeyer also said the euro would not provide a solution to the various challenges ahead for global markets.

"It is for this reason that the selection of suitable (European Economic and Monetary Union) participants on the basis of convincing and sustainable fulfilment of the convergence criteria is so important," he said.

The Bundesbank has steadfastly called for durable fulfilment of the Maastricht criteria, particularly as concern mounts that key players in Europe, including Germany, look set to struggle to meet the EMU goals this year.

The greatest risks are seen in the field of public finance, with Maastricht calling on countries to keep their budget deficits at no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and debt at no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Tietmeyer noted that Germany and many other countries in Europe had a higher degree of monetary stability than they had enjoyed for years.
"But we must not fool ourselves. Inflation danger is never "dead as a doornail" and securing monetary stability remains an ongoing task," he said.
The Bundesbank chief also repeated his welcome for Britian's new Labour government's move this week to give the Bank of England more autonomy on its monetary policy decisions.

That decision had brought conditions for monetary policy in Germany and Britain closer together, he said, although the degree of independence granted to the English central bank did not yet meet Maastricht criteria.
"But Britain obviously does not want to participate at least in the beginning of monetary union," Tietmeyer said.
